title: Better Decisions · Episode 2
chapters: Outcome bias: why good decisions can end badly
The framing effect: same facts, different choices

units.t: Better Decisions. Episode two.
In this episode: Understanding risk, Outcome bias: why good decisions can end badly and The framing effect: same facts, different choices.
Part one. Understanding risk.
People fear sharks and plane crashes, then drive home tired without a second thought.
Our risk radar is badly calibrated, and it can be fixed.
Why we misjudge risk.
Humans didn't evolve to read statistics.
We judge danger with fast, emotional shortcuts.
Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the availability heuristic: we rate something as more likely when examples spring easily to mind.
Shark attacks and plane crashes get saturation news coverage, so they feel common.
Heart disease, falls at home and car crashes rarely make headlines, so they feel ordinary.
Paul Slovic and other researchers found we also fear risks that feel uncontrollable, unfamiliar or imposed on us far more than risks we choose.
Australia records a handful of fatal shark bites a year, yet around 300 or more people drown, many in rivers, lakes and backyard pools.
Dread risks.
A 'dread risk' is a rare event that kills many people at once, such as a plane crash or terrorist attack.
It triggers fear far beyond its statistical danger.
After the September 11 attacks in 2001, many Americans avoided flying and drove instead.
Psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer estimated the extra driving caused roughly 1,500 additional road deaths in the following year, more than the passengers killed on the four hijacked planes.
Australia's road toll runs at roughly 1,100 to 1,300 deaths a year, plus tens of thousands of serious injuries.
Qantas has never had a fatal jet accident, and per kilometre, flying on a major airline is many times safer than driving.
The riskiest part of a trip is often the drive to the airport.
Relative versus absolute.
Headlines love relative risk: 'X doubles your risk of Y'.
But doubling a tiny risk still leaves a tiny risk.
In 1995, UK authorities warned that newer contraceptive pills doubled the risk of a type of blood clot.
The absolute increase was roughly from 1 in 7,000 women to 2 in 7,000.
Many women stopped taking the pill, and researchers later linked the scare to a rise in unplanned pregnancies and abortions, which carry their own risks.
Whenever you hear 'increases risk by 50 per cent', ask: 50 per cent of what?
How many people out of 1,000 or 10,000 are actually affected?
Ignoring base rates.
The base rate is how often something happens in the first place, and we routinely ignore it when a good story comes along.
Kahneman and Tversky described 'Steve': shy, tidy and helpful, with a passion for detail.
Is he more likely a librarian or a farmer?
Most people say librarian, because he fits the stereotype.
But in the United States there were more than 20 male farmers for every male librarian, so Steve is far more likely to farm.
The same trap catches us with a 'sure thing' share tip, a start-up that looks like the next big success, or a stranger who 'looks suspicious'.
Before judging by fit, ask how common it is.
Deciding better.
Good risk thinking asks four questions.
How likely is it, in absolute terms?
How bad would it be, and is it reversible?
Compared with what, including the risk of the alternative?
Can I cheaply reduce it?
Say '3 in 1,000' rather than '0.
3 per cent', and notice when a vivid story is doing the work data should.
The biggest killers are slow and familiar: heart disease, dementia, cancers, smoking and inactivity, plus falls among older Australians.
Put effort into seatbelts, not driving tired, pool fences, sun protection and health checks.
Zero risk doesn't exist; doing nothing carries risk too.
Researchers compare activities in 'micromorts', a one-in-a-million chance of death.
For medical choices, ask your doctor to explain the numbers in plain terms.
The key idea: We judge risk by how vivid and emotional it feels, not by how likely it is.
Part two. Outcome bias: why good decisions can end badly.
A coach made one of the most criticised calls in sport, and a poker player says we judged it all wrong.
Learn to tell a smart choice from a lucky one.
The worst call ever.
In February 2015 the Seattle Seahawks were seconds from winning the Super Bowl.
Trailing the New England Patriots by four points, they had the ball about a metre from the line with 26 seconds left.
Most fans expected a handoff to their powerful running back.
Instead, coach Pete Carroll called a pass.
It was intercepted, and the Patriots won.
Headlines called it one of the worst calls in the game's history.
Yet some analysts argued it was reasonable: interceptions that close to the line are rare, and an incomplete pass would stop the clock.
Former poker player Annie Duke, in her 2018 book Thinking in Bets, calls judging by results alone ‘resulting’.
In poker you can play a hand perfectly and still lose to the last card.
In life there are fewer hands and messier information.
The surgeon experiment.
In 1988 the psychologists Jonathan Baron and John Hershey gave volunteers descriptions of decisions made under uncertainty, such as a doctor's choice about whether to go ahead with a risky operation.
Everyone received the same information that had been available to the decision-maker at the time.
The only thing that changed was the outcome: in some versions the patient lived, and in others the patient died.
People rated the decision itself as worse, and the decision-maker as less competent, when the outcome was bad.
Yet the choice had been made with exactly the same knowledge.
Baron and Hershey called this outcome bias.
Four kinds of result.
Picture a simple grid.
A good decision with a good outcome is a deserved success.
A good decision with a bad outcome is bad luck.
A bad decision with a bad outcome is a predictable failure.
And a bad decision with a good outcome is a lucky escape, which may be the most dangerous of all.
Think of someone who drives home after too many drinks and arrives safely.
The outcome teaches them nothing useful, or worse, teaches them it was fine.
Each lucky escape can make the next risky choice feel safer.
Outcome bias collapses these four boxes into two: it worked, so it was right; it failed, so it was wrong.
Hindsight makes it worse.
Outcome bias has a close relative: hindsight bias, the feeling that we ‘knew it all along’.
In the 1970s the psychologist Baruch Fischhoff showed that once people learnt how an event turned out, they judged that outcome to have been more predictable than people who hadn't been told.
Their memories of what they had predicted earlier also shifted towards what actually happened.
Together these biases make the world seem more orderly than it really is.
They also make us unfair judges.
Workers, doctors, pilots and leaders can be blamed for bad outcomes they could not reasonably have foreseen, while people who took foolish risks and got away with them can be rewarded and promoted.
Judge the process.
The fix is to judge decisions by the process behind them.
Ask: what did we know at the time?
What options did we consider?
Did we think about the risks and how likely they were?
Was there information we could reasonably have gathered but didn't?
Armies, hospitals and airlines have long used structured reviews after events, and these work best when they examine successes and failures with the same honesty.
A simple personal tool is a decision journal.
Before an important choice, write down what you expect to happen and why.
Later, compare that with what actually happened.
Over time you'll see whether your judgement is sound, or whether you've simply been lucky.
The key idea: Judging a decision only by how it turned out, which poker players call ‘resulting’, is a mistake.
Part three. The framing effect: same facts, different choices.
Would you choose a treatment with a 90 per cent survival rate?
What about one with a 10 per cent death rate?
They're identical, yet the wording changes what people choose.
An imaginary outbreak.
In 1981 the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman published a now-famous problem.
Imagine a disease outbreak expected to kill 600 people.
One group chose between two programs.
With Program A, 200 people will be saved.
With Program B, there's a one-third chance all 600 are saved and a two-thirds chance no-one is saved.
Most chose A, the sure thing.
A second group got the same choice in different words.
With Program C, 400 people will die.
With Program D, there's a one-third chance nobody dies and a two-thirds chance all 600 die.
Now most chose D, the gamble.
Yet A and C describe exactly the same outcome, as do B and D.
Gains safe, losses risky.
The outbreak problem revealed a pattern that Kahneman and Tversky built into their prospect theory.
When outcomes are described as gains, such as lives saved, people tend to be cautious and prefer a certain result.
When the same outcomes are described as losses, such as deaths, people become more willing to gamble to avoid a sure loss.
Part of the reason is loss aversion: losses tend to feel more painful than equivalent gains feel good, with many studies putting the ratio at roughly two to one, though estimates vary.
Logically, the wording should make no difference.
Psychologically, the frame sets the reference point against which everything else is judged.
Doctors are not immune.
You might hope experts would see through framing.
In a 1982 study in the New England Journal of Medicine, Barbara McNeil and colleagues, including Tversky, asked people to choose between surgery and radiation therapy for lung cancer.
Surgery carried a higher risk of dying during or soon after treatment, but better long-term survival.
When the results were presented as chances of surviving, surgery looked more attractive than when the very same results were described as chances of dying.
The effect appeared among patients, among students, and among physicians.
Since then, many guides to communicating medical risk have encouraged presenting figures in more than one way, for example giving both survival and death rates together.
Framing in shops and news.
In a 1988 study, Irwin Levin and Gary Gaeth asked people to evaluate minced beef described as either ‘75 per cent lean’ or ‘25 per cent fat’.
Same meat, but the ‘lean’ version was rated better quality and less greasy.
The gap shrank when people tasted the beef, though it didn't vanish.
Yoghurt is ‘95 per cent fat free’ rather than ‘5 per cent fat’.
A fee is a ‘discount for paying cash’ rather than a ‘surcharge for paying by card’.
A broader kind of framing highlights different aspects of an issue.
In a 1997 study, readers of a news story about a planned Ku Klux Klan rally were more tolerant of it when it was framed as free speech than as a threat to public order.
Defusing the frame.
You can't avoid frames, because every description has to start somewhere.
But you can learn to notice them.
When you face an important choice, deliberately flip the wording: if you're told nine out of ten customers are satisfied, remind yourself that one in ten isn't.
If a deal is framed as avoiding a loss, ask how it looks as a plain gain.
Turn percentages into concrete counts, such as ‘out of 100 people like me, how many?’
This makes risks much easier to compare.
Be especially wary when someone else has chosen the frame for you and stands to gain from your decision.
And when you present information to others, giving both frames is often the fairest thing you can do.
The key idea: Describing identical options as lives saved or lives lost flips people's choices.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does the availability heuristic lead us to do?
Answer. Judge a risk as likelier when examples come easily.
Question two. What does ‘resulting’ mean?
Answer. Judging a choice only by its result.
Question three. In the outbreak problem, why is the switch in people's choices surprising?
Answer. A and C described the very same outcome.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
